parts.problem_md:
Read Text C, *The big adventure*, in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_cswTDKdfSQy7hG9t/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-May-June%2F0500_s23_in_13.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Question 3(a-d).

**3(c)** Use **one** example from the text below to explain how the writer suggests Andy's attitude to the coast near Ilhabela.

**Use your own words in your explanation.**

"The coast just north of Ilhabela is punctuated by pretty, tranquil coves. Abi and I were looking forward to a week of snorkelling and generally lounging about. But first, Dael pointed out, a storm was coming. The channel between Ilhabela and the mainland is long and thin. Hills on both sides provide the perfect funnel for the strong winds that develop over the South Atlantic. The water is also very shallow, conducive to close, steep waves."
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The writer uses the image of the “perfect funnel for the strong winds” to convey how Andy's relaxed attitude gives way to a sense of being trapped by the approaching danger. The word “funnel” suggests that the hills on either side of the channel squeeze and concentrate the wind, channelling its full force directly towards the boat, so that there is no way to avoid it. The adjective “perfect” is quietly ominous: it implies that the landscape is ideally shaped to intensify the storm, as if nature itself is conspiring against the sailors. This precise, almost technical description makes the threat feel measured and inevitable rather than dramatic, which is somehow more frightening, and it shows how Andy's earlier hopes of “snorkelling and generally lounging about” have been replaced by an uneasy awareness of risk.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - "pretty, tranquil coves": idyllic; calm and peaceful; welcoming; presents the coast as a reward to look forward to
> - "looking forward to a week of snorkelling and generally lounging about": eager anticipation; relaxed; carefree; ready to enjoy a holiday after the crossing
> - "a storm was coming": abrupt change; warning; sense of threat undercutting the relaxed mood
> - "perfect funnel for the strong winds": hills concentrate the wind; entrapment; no escape; landscape intensifies the danger; ominous
> - "very shallow" / "close, steep waves": precise, technical detail; makes the threat feel measured and inevitable; dangerous conditions
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The answer selects one example and explains in depth how the image of the “perfect funnel” conveys Andy's shift from relaxed anticipation to an uneasy sense of entrapment and danger. The explanation is in the candidate's own words throughout and shows clear understanding of how language creates effect, earning Level 5 (4-5 marks).
> 
> **Reading**
> 
> | Level | Marks | Description |
> |---|---|---|
> | 3 | 4-5 | Clear understanding of the writer's use of language |
> | 2 | 2-3 | Some understanding of the writer's use of language |
> | 1 | 1 | Limited understanding of the writer's use of language |
> | 0 | 0 | No creditable content |

parts.problem_md:
Read Text C, *The lost cave*, in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_2YZsk5M9PRXQVd4V/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-Oct-Nov%2F0500_w23_in_12.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Question 3(a-d).

**3(c)** Use **one** example from the text below to explain how the writer suggests Rohaan's feelings when he first sees the cave entrance.

**Use your own words in your explanation.**

“He looked at what was left of the rock face. A gaping hole stared defiantly back at him, as if inviting a stand-off. Rohaan dropped his eyes to break the gaze and received an immense surprise. Half a metre from the base was the floor of a cave entrance. It was surely inviting him to look inside.”
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The writer uses personification in the phrase “A gaping hole stared defiantly back at him” to convey Rohaan's sense of shock and unease when he first sees the cave entrance. By describing the hole as if it can “stare”, the writer makes the cave seem almost alive and aggressive, as though it is confronting Rohaan and challenging him to react. The adverb “defiantly” reinforces this hostility, suggesting the cave is bold and unyielding, refusing to be ignored. The image transforms an inanimate opening in the rock into an opponent, capturing the way Rohaan feels momentarily overpowered and intimidated by his sudden discovery, frozen with surprise and unsure whether to advance or retreat.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - "A gaping hole stared defiantly back at him": huge space; hostile encounter; looking back at him; expression of astonishment; wide open mouth
> - "as if inviting a stand-off": trying to lure him into a fight; challenging; combative; taunting; waiting for someone to make the first move
> - "dropped his eyes to break the gaze": looked down/away; disengaging from the challenge; feels intimidated; cave is superior
> - "received an immense surprise": got a shock; hugely unexpected; could hardly contain his disbelief
> - "surely inviting him to look inside": seems to be asking him in; obvious entrance to something; wants him to explore; tempted; conflicted - excited but nervous
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The answer selects one example and explains in depth how the personification “A gaping hole stared defiantly back at him” conveys Rohaan's shock, unease and sense of being overpowered. The explanation is in the candidate's own words throughout and shows clear understanding of how language creates effect, earning full marks (5/5).
>

parts.problem_md:
Read Text C, *The violinist*, in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_ChRcRRsMgCyw6kck/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-Oct-Nov%2F0500_w23_in_13.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Question 3(a-d).

**3(c)** Use **one** example from the text below to explain how the writer suggests Seth's experiences and feelings when he plays the violin. **Use your own words** in your explanation.

“Violin in hand, Seth stopped four strings with his fingers, and drew the bow over them with one rapid sweep. He'd produced a rich chord. He was surprised by how strong the sound was. He raised his bow again and the violin replied enchantingly. Seth felt excitement shooting through him.”
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The writer personifies the violin when it “replied enchantingly”, suggesting that the instrument is entering into a conversation or relationship with Seth. The verb “replied” implies that the violin is responding to him as if it were alive, transforming a solitary act into a kind of dialogue. The adverb “enchantingly” adds a magical, almost spellbinding quality to the sound, hinting that Seth is captivated and entranced by what he has created. Together, the words convey both the beauty of the music and the sense of mutual connection Seth feels, as though the violin is welcoming him and rewarding his first attempt with something wonderful. This captures the wonder and excitement of his discovery.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - “one rapid sweep”: quick; large movement; skilled musician / confidence as a musician
> - “produced a rich chord”: made a musical sound; full-bodied / deep / beautiful / mellow; pleasure at the sound; high quality / luxurious
> - “surprised by how strong the sound was”: unexpectedly loud; powerful / forceful / potent; impressed
> - “replied enchantingly”: as if talking back to him / conversation; responding to being played; melodious, harmonious; magical qualities / entranced; delighted
> - “felt excitement shooting through him”: great surge of enthusiasm; eagerness; rush of pleasure; powerful feeling
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The answer selects one example and explains in depth how the personification “replied enchantingly” creates a magical sense of connection between Seth and the violin. The explanation is in the candidate's own words throughout and demonstrates clear understanding of how language works, earning full marks (5/5).
>

**3(c)** Use **one** example from the text below to explain how the writer suggests Edgar's thoughts and feelings at that time.

**Use your own words in your explanation.**

“‘I've got a report to write for the boss tonight!’ huffed Edgar. ‘Apparently she doesn't know what our job involves. Hah!’

He marched towards the group. ‘Good morning. Your documents, please, so I can make sure they are in order before you drop your luggage off.’ Edgar flipped through identity documents with the dexterity of a master player shuffling a deck of cards, before surveying the three suitcases. ‘Take it you packed those suitcases yourselves and they haven't been out of sight since you got here? Go to the roped area over there. Shouldn't be too long to wait.’”
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The simile “Edgar flipped through identity documents with the dexterity of a master player shuffling a deck of cards” reveals Edgar's mixture of efficiency and self-satisfaction. The comparison to a card player suggests he performs this task with the casual, almost theatrical confidence of someone who has done it thousands of times - his hands move quickly and deftly without conscious effort. The word "dexterity" emphasises physical skill and precision, implying that Edgar takes pride in how smoothly he operates even when irritated. The image also carries a hint of showmanship, as if Edgar is performing for Jeswin's benefit. This suggests that despite his exasperation about the report, he is still firmly in control of his professional role.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - “huffed Edgar”: tone is annoyed; feels report is an unreasonable imposition; exclamation mark emphasises exasperation
> - “Apparently she doesn't know what our job involves. Hah!”: sarcastic; contemptuous of boss; “Hah!” is dismissive; self-pity
> - “marched towards the group”: confident and/or annoyed; officious; purposeful; showing off to Jeswin
> - “flipped through identity documents with the dexterity of a master player shuffling a deck of cards”: proficient; done it many times; efficient; showing his skills
> - “surveying the three suitcases”: scanning with machine-like efficiency; expert; in control
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The response selects a relevant quotation and analyses multiple elements - the simile, the word "dexterity", the implications of showmanship - in sustained, precise explanation. It moves beyond surface meaning to explore what the image suggests about Edgar's state of mind, earning Level 5 (4-5 marks).
> 
> **Reading**
>

"And that was it: training was over! I'd never pushed a button, had only the flimsiest concept how a ski lift even worked, much less how to fix one if something went wrong, didn't know how to test the equipment, use the radio in case of emergency or assist guests on and off the lift. Ski lifts spin all day, every hour transporting skiers and riders of all ability levels up the mountain. I didn't know how many things I didn't know about my new job - but suspected there were plenty."

### Model answer

The writer uses the repetition of “didn't know” to convey Tony's growing sense of helplessness and anxiety about his new job. The phrase is used three times in quick succession, and this cumulative effect mirrors the way his worries pile up on top of one another: the more Tony lists what he does not know, the more exposed and unprepared he feels. The final admission that he “didn't know how many things I didn't know” is especially effective, because it suggests that his ignorance is so vast he cannot even measure it. This captures both his genuine anxiety and a note of wry self-awareness, as he recognises with rueful honesty just how far out of his depth he is.

> - "And that was it: training was over!": abrupt ending; shock; disbelief that so little has been covered
> - "flimsiest concept": very limited understanding; weak, fragile knowledge
> - repetition of "didn't know": building anxiety and helplessness; cumulative effect
> - "all ability levels" / "every hour": relentless responsibility; the safety of many people; scale of the task
> - "suspected there were plenty": self-aware; wry humour mixed with genuine anxiety
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**

**3(c)** Use **one **example from the text below to explain how the writer suggests Anna's attitude during the radio interview.

**Use your own words** in your explanation.

"I was sitting, star-struck, in the Southland FM's Invercargill studio, marvelling at radio host Rach's seemingly exotic accent. I already loved the way that people here pronounced my name as: “Inna!” I grinned widely from behind a microphone bigger than my head.

Rach continued: “So, are you brave or stupid?”

“Perhaps both,” I laughed enigmatically. “And excited.”"
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The phrase "grinned widely from behind a microphone bigger than my head" reveals Anna's uninhibited delight during the interview. The verb "grinned" suggests a broad, unself-conscious smile - not a polite, composed expression, but an almost childlike beam of happiness. The detail that the microphone is "bigger than my head" is comic and self-deprecating: the oversize equipment dwarfs Anna, making her seem out of her depth, yet she grins with total abandon anyway. This suggests she is so swept up in the excitement that any self-consciousness is completely forgotten. The image paints Anna as someone not performing confidence but genuinely overwhelmed with joy - star-struck and carefree. This naive enthusiasm is central to her characterisation throughout the extract.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use:
> 
> - "sitting, star-struck": admired Rach; over-awed; dazzled; unable to communicate effectively; suggests she has been frozen in admiration
> - "marvelling at... seemingly exotic accent": Rach's accent was unusual to Anna; she is amazed by the difference; suggests she is over-reacting or romanticising the experience
> - "grinned widely from behind a microphone bigger than my head": smiled broadly; open and positive; thoroughly enjoying the experience; comic sense of being out of her depth; cannot contain her joy
> - "laughed enigmatically": trying to appear mysterious; may suggest bravado; playing the role of a celebrity adventurer; has not thought through the implications of what she is about to do
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The response selects one apt quotation and explains how multiple specific elements of the language - the verb “grinned”, the comic detail of the microphone's size, the lack of self-consciousness - combine to suggest Anna's attitude. The explanation adds meaning to the original rather than paraphrasing it, and is written in the candidate's own words. This earns Level 5 (4-5 marks).

### Model answer

The writer uses the phrase “swarmed and buzzed around her” to vividly convey the overwhelming, frantic reaction of the townspeople. By using this insect imagery, the writer compares the crowd to a massive, excitable hive of bees. The word “swarmed” suggests that the people moved in huge, uncontrollable hordes, drawn irresistibly and physically close to Annie. Furthermore, “buzzed” captures the loud, chaotic hum of their excited chatter, emphasising how they circled her in a noisy, fanatic manner that was almost suffocating or annoying in its intensity.

> - demanding autographs: asking for signed mementos, expecting them, more than is reasonable, fanatical
